title: The true friend
hook: false friends and true friends, and how to tell them apart

segments.voice: Yesterday: where wealth drains away, and your line, six leaks. Which leak did you plug? One of them was bad company, and today the Buddha tells Sigala how to spot it. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

You're moving apartments. You post in the group chat: anyone free Saturday? One friend replies with ten heart emojis and a long message about how much they wish they could. One says they'll be there, then asks if you can lend them your car next week. One goes quiet. And one just shows up at eight with coffee and a dolly, and stays until the last box is in. The Sigalovada has a name for every one of them. Today: the true friend.
screen: `ANYONE FREE SATURDAY?` → `HEARTS, FAVORS, SILENCE.` → `ONE SHOWS UP AT EIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha tells Sigala, there are four who look like friends and aren't. The taker, who gives little and asks a lot, and helps only out of fear or for his own gain. The talker, all words: he's generous about the past and the future, but when you need something now, he points to his bad luck. The flatterer, who agrees with whatever you do, good or bad, praises you to your face, and runs you down behind your back. And the companion in wasting: your partner for drinking, for roaming at night, for shows and for gambling. Then four true friends, each with a fine detail. The helper: he looks after you when you're careless, guards your things, is a refuge when you're afraid, and when there's a job to do, gives you twice what you asked for. The one who's the same in good times and bad: he tells you his secrets, keeps yours, doesn't leave you when things go wrong, and would give his life for you. The one who points the way: he keeps you from wrong, encourages what's good, tells you what you haven't heard, and shows you the way to a good life. And the one who cares: he doesn't celebrate your bad luck, he's glad at your good luck, stops others when they speak ill of you, and praises those who speak well of you. Notice how practical this is. Every test is something you can watch for. And notice the mirror in it: the same list tells you what kind of friend to be.
screen: `THE TAKER, THE TALKER, THE FLATTERER.` · `THE HELPER GIVES TWICE.` · `THE SAME IN GOOD AND BAD.` · `THE ONE WHO POINTS THE WAY.` · then, large: `THE FRIEND IN NEED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let one true friend come to mind. Someone who showed up. Picture the moment: what they did, how it felt. Breathe that gratitude in. Then ask, quietly, which of the four true friends you are to someone. The helper? The steady one? The one who points the way? The one who cares? After the bell, if you like, send that friend a message of thanks. The bell holds the time.
The true friend. In DN 31, four false friends and four true ones: the helper, the steady one, the one who points the way, and the one who cares. Today's word.
Your line: the friend in need. Today, thank one true friend for a specific time they showed up, and be that friend for someone else. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many traditions teach the Sigalovada's eight kinds of friend to young people and families, and the Buddha's wider teaching calls good friendship, kalyanamittata, the whole of the holy life.

fork.setup: you need help now. a friend says how much he'd have helped last month, and how he'll help next year, but today he's unlucky. which kind of friend is he?
fork.reveal: the talker: generous about past and future, empty in the present.

original.note: Pali mitta: friend. a true friend is called suhada, good-hearted.

trapdoor: what you thought: a friend is anyone who's nice to you.
what it means: DN 31 gives eight kinds of friend, four false and four true, each with tests you can watch.
what a scholar hears: the Sigalovada contrasts mitta-patirupaka (counterfeit friends) with suhada mitta (good-hearted friends), four of each with four marks apiece.
